Do Any of These Feel Familiar?

The Six Reasons Claims Actually Get Denied

Payer-specific denial trends repeat themselves. Once you know the pattern, you can fix it at the source instead of resubmitting the same mistake.

The problem: A wrong birth date or a misspelled name seems minor, but these eligibility verification errors cause real hold-ups in getting paid.

The fix: Clean claims submission every time. Errors are caught before the claim goes out, using coding-and-eligibility checks that flag mismatches instantly.

The problem: Payers check ICD-10, CPT and HCPCS accuracy closely. One wrong code, or a flagged modifier misuse, triggers a coding denial.

The fix: Regular coding accuracy audits ensure the codes billed match the care given and what payers expect, cutting rejections and avoiding upcoding or downcoding flags.

The problem: Payer filing deadlines are strict cutoffs. Submit a claim late and the payer often simply won't pay, no matter how clean the claim is.

The fix: Systematic denial tracking against every payer's deadline keeps A/R teams ahead of the clock and prevents write-offs caused purely by late filing.

The problem: A claim that looks like it was sent twice gets an automatic, fast denial, delaying payment for a legitimate service.

The fix: Claim scrubbing before submission catches duplicate entries, double-checking every claim is accurate before it ever reaches a payer.

The problem: Services that need a pre-authorization green light get an immediate denial if that step is missed. It's one of the most common sources of revenue leakage.

The fix: A clear authorization tracking process confirms approval is in hand before service is delivered, removing this denial category almost entirely.

The problem: When a patient has more than one insurance plan, figuring out who pays first gets tricky. COB mistakes cause denials, extra follow-up work, and sometimes surprise patient bills.

The fix: Early benefits verification routes claims to the correct payer in the correct order the first time, cutting COB-driven delays before they start.

Our Denial Management Workflow

Nine Steps, From First Flag to Final Resolution

A solid denial management process is what keeps a denial rate near or below 2%, meaning the vast majority of claims get paid without a fight.

  1. 1

    Spotting Denied Claims

    Claim tracking systems and remittance advice (ERAs/EOBs) are reviewed carefully to flag any denial and kick off resolution without delay.

  2. 2

    Sorting Out the Denials

    Each denial is classified as technical (coding error), clinical (medical necessity) or administrative (payer policy, eligibility), then routed to the right specialist.

  3. 3

    Finding the Real Reason

    Denial codes, CARC/RARC messages and payer-specific requirements are examined closely to understand exactly why the claim was denied.

  4. 4

    Tracking Trends

    Denial rates, common reasons and other KPIs are tracked using revenue cycle analytics, feeding directly into process improvements and prevention efforts.

  5. 5

    Appealing and Resubmitting

    Clinical input for medical justification and coding corrections come together so every appeal is strong and aligned with compliance rules.

  6. 6

    Meeting Appeal Deadlines

    Appeals are submitted strictly within each payer's timeframe. Missing a deadline means an automatic rejection, so timeliness is treated as non-negotiable.

  7. 7

    Following Up and Checking Status

    Appealed claims are tracked in real time, with follow-up to payers for updates and any extra information a decision might require.

  8. 8

    Handling the Tough Cases

    For complex or high-dollar denials that resist initial appeals, peer-to-peer reviews or secondary appeals and payer-level discussions secure a fair reconsideration.

  9. 9

    Analysis and Feedback

    Clear compliance and trend reports feed insights back into your RCM, helping the practice understand patterns and strengthen overall financial health.

Hospital Denial Management
